# SNAC-Go

Source: https://github.com/tcpipuk/snac-go/blob/main/README.md

# SNAC-Go


Pure Go implementation of the SNAC neural audio codec decoder for text-to-speech applications.

## Overview

SNAC-Go decodes multi-scale neural audio codes into high-quality audio waveforms. It integrates with
[llama-go](https://github.com/tcpipuk/llama-go) to enable complete Go-based text-to-speech using
models like Orpheus TTS, with no Python runtime dependencies.

## Features

- **Pure Go implementation** - No CGO, Python, or PyTorch dependencies
- **SNAC 24kHz model** - Speech-optimised decoder (19.8M parameters)
- **Hierarchical decoding** - Multi-scale vector quantisation with 3 codebook levels
- **Production-ready** - Ground-truth verified against upstream Python SNAC (MSE < 1e-5)

## Installation

```bash
go get github.com/tcpipuk/snac-go
```

## Quick start

```go
package main

import (
    "github.com/tcpipuk/snac-go/snac"
    "log"
)

func main() {
    // Load SNAC decoder with 24kHz model
    decoder, err := snac.NewDecoder("hubertsiuzdak/snac_24khz")
    if err != nil {
        log.Fatal(err)
    }

    // Decode SNAC tokens to audio
    // tokens is [3][]int representing 3 hierarchical codebook levels
    audio, err := decoder.Decode(tokens)
    if err != nil {
        log.Fatal(err)
    }

    // Write to WAV file
    if err := writeWAV("output.wav", audio, 24000); err != nil {
        log.Fatal(err)
    }
}
```

## Why Go?

The Python SNAC decoder is ~474 lines whilst this is nearly 4700. We want pure Go for TTS
([llama-go](https://github.com/tcpipuk/llama-go) runs
[Orpheus](https://huggingface.co/canopylabs/orpheus-3b-0.1-ft), snac-go decodes audio), but PyTorch
does the heavy lifting in Python - convolutions and attention get implemented manually using
Gorgonia. [GoMLX](https://github.com/gomlx/gomlx) would shrink this significantly, but it's pre-v1.0
with API instability. Current approach is pragmatic: reliable pure Go now, but ready to migrate when
GoMLX stabilises.

## Documentation

See [Architecture Guide](./docs/architecture.md) for technical details about how SNAC decoder works.

## Status

- ✅ Architecture implementation complete (~4700 lines pure Go)
- ✅ Weight loading and conversion tooling ready
- ✅ Ground truth verification complete (151 tests passing, MSE < 1e-5)
- ✅ Production-ready decoder verified against Python SNAC
- ⏳ API subject to change before v1.0

# SNAC Decoder Architecture

Source: https://github.com/tcpipuk/snac-go/blob/main/docs/architecture.md

# SNAC Decoder Architecture

## Overview

SNAC (Multi-Scale Neural Audio Codec) uses hierarchical vector quantisation to represent audio as
discrete tokens at multiple temporal resolutions. The decoder network transforms these tokens back
into high-quality audio waveforms through a series of upsampling and attention operations.

The architecture is pure feedforward with no recurrence, enabling efficient parallel processing and
real-time inference.

## Hierarchical Vector Quantisation

SNAC represents audio using four levels of discrete codes, each capturing different temporal
resolutions:

**Input format:**

- **Level 0:** Coarsest features (~80ms per token, ~12 tokens/second)
- **Level 1:** Mid-level features (~40ms per token, ~24 tokens/second)
- **Level 2:** Fine features (~20ms per token, ~48 tokens/second)
- **Level 3:** Finest features (~10ms per token, ~96 tokens/second)

Each level uses a codebook of 4096 possible tokens (12-bit discrete codes). The multi-scale approach
captures both coarse structure (prosody, phonemes) and fine detail (acoustic texture, speaker
characteristics) efficiently.

### Codebook Structure

Each codebook level consists of:

- 4096 embedding vectors (codebook size)
- 8-dimensional embeddings per code (codebook dimension)
- Stride factors: [8, 4, 2, 1] for temporal upsampling
- Independent lookups per level

The decoder combines these levels through residual connections, allowing each scale to refine the
reconstruction progressively.

## Decoder Network

The decoder transforms hierarchical tokens to audio through several stages:

### 1. Vector Quantisation Decoder

**Embedding lookup**: Each token index is mapped to its corresponding 8-dimensional embedding vector
from the appropriate codebook.

**Projection and upsampling**: Each level undergoes:

- Conv1d projection from codebook dimension (8) to latent dimension (64)
- Stride-based upsampling using transposed convolution
- Upsampling factors: Level 0 (8×), Level 1 (4×), Level 2 (2×), Level 3 (1×)

**Residual summation**: All upsampled levels are summed element-wise to produce the unified latent
representation for the decoder network.

### 2. Initial Projection

Conv1d transforms the latent representation (64 channels) to decoder dimension (1536 channels),
providing sufficient capacity for the decoder blocks.

### 3. Multi-Head Attention (LocalMHA)

Window-based local attention mechanism:

**Architecture:**

- 12 attention heads
- 128 dimensions per head (1536 total)
- Window size: 32 samples (local attention only)
- Rotary position embeddings (RoPE) for position awareness

**Operation:** Standard multi-head attention with Q, K, V projections, but attention is restricted
to a local window of 32 samples. This reduces computational cost from O(n²) to O(n·w) whilst
maintaining quality for audio where local context dominates.

**RoPE (Rotary Position Embeddings):** Embeds positional information by rotating Q and K vectors in
a position-dependent manner. Precomputed sine/cosine tables enable efficient position encoding
without learned parameters.

### 4. Decoder Blocks

Four decoder blocks progressively upsample the latent representation to audio resolution:

**Each block contains:**

- Snake activation for non-linearity
- Transposed convolution for 5× upsampling (rates: [5, 5, 3, 3])
- Three residual units with dilated convolutions
- Skip connections preserving gradient flow

**Snake activation:** `x + (1/α) * sin²(α * x)` provides smooth non-linearity with learnable
frequency parameter α. This activation works particularly well for audio signals.

**Upsampling progression:**

1. Block 0: 1536 → 768 channels, 5× upsampling
2. Block 1: 768 → 384 channels, 5× upsampling
3. Block 2: 384 → 128 channels, 3× upsampling
4. Block 3: 128 → 64 channels, 3× upsampling

Total upsampling: 5 × 5 × 3 × 3 = 225× from latent to audio rate.

### 5. Output Layer

Final Conv1d reduces 64 channels to 1 (mono audio), followed by tanh activation to bound output to
[-1, 1] range. The result is a 24kHz audio waveform ready for playback or storage.

## Model Configuration (SNAC 24kHz)

The 24kHz speech-optimised model uses these parameters:

```json
{
  "sampling_rate": 24000,
  "encoder_dim": 64,
  "encoder_rates": [3, 3, 5, 5],
  "latent_dim": 64,
  "decoder_dim": 1536,
  "decoder_rates": [5, 5, 3, 3],
  "attn_window_size": 32,
  "codebook_size": 4096,
  "codebook_dim": 8,
  "vq_strides": [8, 4, 2, 1]
}
```

**Model size:**

- Parameters: 19.8M (decoder only)
- File size: ~76 MB (float32)
- Bitrate: 0.98 kbps
- Sample rate: 24kHz mono

## Implementation Details

### Weight Normalisation

The upstream PyTorch model uses weight normalisation for convolutional layers. During model loading,
we fold the normalisation parameters (direction and magnitude) into the weight tensors themselves.
This eliminates runtime normalisation overhead whilst maintaining numerical equivalence.

### Numerical Considerations

- **Floating point**: float32 throughout (matches PyTorch default)
- **Numerical stability**: Subtract maximum before softmax in attention
- **Tensor layouts**: Channel-first [batch, channels, sequence] for convolutions
- **Attention tensors**: [batch, heads, sequence, head_dim] layout

### Computational Efficiency

The decoder is designed for efficient inference:

- **Pure feedforward**: No recurrent connections or iterative refinement
- **Local attention**: O(n·w) instead of O(n²) attention complexity
- **Parallel processing**: All operations support batched inference
- **Memory efficiency**: ~500MB peak memory for typical inference

### Streaming Capability

The architecture supports streaming inference by processing audio in chunks:

- Each SNAC frame (7 tokens) generates ~100ms of audio
- Fixed upsampling ratios enable predictable latency
- Local attention window (32 samples) requires minimal context overlap
- Suitable for real-time TTS applications

### Primary Sources

- **SNAC paper**:
  [Multi-Scale Neural Audio Codec (arXiv:2410.14411)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.14411)
- **Official implementation**: [hubertsiuzdak/snac](https://github.com/hubertsiuzdak/snac)
- **Pretrained models**: [HuggingFace - hubertsiuzdak](https://huggingface.co/hubertsiuzdak)

### Related Work

- **RoFormer**: Rotary position embeddings [arXiv:2104.09864](https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.09864)
- **Snake activation**: [arXiv:2006.08195](https://arxiv.org/abs/2006.08195)
- **Weight normalisation**: [arXiv:1602.07868](https://arxiv.org/abs/1602.07868)

### Integration

- **Orpheus TTS**: Multi-voice TTS model outputting SNAC tokens

- **llama-go**: Go bindings for llama.cpp enabling Orpheus TTS in Go
  - [Repository](https://github.com/tcpipuk/llama-go)
